candidates.title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Yang S, Wang H, et al.
candidates.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain. PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis. STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1. METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care (PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, satisfaction, adverse events, and costs. RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) (Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was maintained. CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-impact RCT in AJSM comparing standardized PRP pathway versus conventional care for knee OA with 240 patients and clinically meaningful outcome differences, directly applicable to practice decisions about PRP administration protocols.
bullets: In adults with early knee osteoarthritis (KL grade I-II), a standardized PRP pathway combining quality-controlled injection, ultrasound guidance, and structured rehab produced meaningfully greater pain and function gains at 12 months than unstructured PRP care.
The standardized pathway cut adverse events by more than half compared to conventional PRP care (15% vs 32%), with no meaningful difference in overall cost.

This trial shows that how PRP is delivered matters as much as the injection itself, but it does not confirm PRP is better than placebo, so patient selection and process standardization remain the key clinical levers.

candidates.title: Comparison of Shoulder Field Anesthesia (SFA) with Interscalene Block (ISB) for Analgesia After Arthroscopic Shoulder Surgery: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Qawasmi F, Gazit T, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: An interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB) is commonly used for analgesia after shoulder surgery but is associated with neurologic and respiratory complications, including hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia (SFA) is a landmark-guided, phrenic nerve-sparing technique that may provide effective analgesia with fewer complications. The purpose of this study was to compare SFA with ISB for pain control after arthroscopic shoulder surgery. We investigated whether SFA would provide noninferior analgesia as measured by cumulative 48-hour postoperative pain scores. METHODS: In this randomized trial, patients undergoing arthroscopic shoulder surgery were assigned to SFA or ISB. Postoperative pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) at 2, 4, 8, 24, and 48 hours. Patient satisfaction was assessed at 48 hours. Other secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, hospital stay, and block-related complications. RESULTS: Eighty patients (mean age, 47.7 ± 15.7 years; 53 men) completed the study. All patients were classified as White; 80% were of Middle Eastern ethnicity. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the SFA and ISB groups. The primary outcome analysis demonstrated a mean difference in the cumulative 48-hour NRS pain score of -0.824 (ISB - SFA), with a 95% confidence interval of -1.853 to 0.206. The upper limit of the confidence interval remained below the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.5 NRS points, demonstrating noninferiority of SFA. ISB provided lower pain scores during the early postoperative period (4 to 8 hours), and pain scores converged thereafter. Hospital stay was shorter in the SFA group. Opioid consumption, patient satisfaction, and oxygen desaturation rates were similar between groups. Two cases of Horner syndrome and 1 respiratory event requiring intensive care occurred in the ISB group; none occurred in the SFA group. CONCLUSIONS: SFA was noninferior to ISB for the prespecified cumulative 48-hour pain end point. ISB provided superior pain relief during the first 4 to 8 hours, but SFA offered a lung-sparing alternative with similar cumulative opioid requirements and patient satisfaction, fewer clinically apparent block-related complications, and a shorter hospital stay. These findings support a risk-benefit framework to guide individualized analgesic selection. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level I. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Clinically relevant comparison of shoulder field anesthesia versus interscalene block in an RCT from JBJS, directly applicable to perioperative analgesia decisions for arthroscopic shoulder surgery with phrenic nerve-sparing implications.
bullets: Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia matched interscalene block for cumulative 48-hour pain control after arthroscopic shoulder surgery in a randomized trial of 80 patients.

Interscalene block provided better pain relief in the first 4 to 8 hours, but scores equalized after that, and the interscalene group had two cases of Horner syndrome and one respiratory ICU admission versus none in the field anesthesia group.

For patients where phrenic nerve palsy or respiratory compromise is a concern, shoulder field anesthesia is a viable alternative to interscalene block with similar opioid use, patient satisfaction, and a shorter hospital stay.

candidates.title: Does a Prior Unsuccessful DAIR Increase the Risk of Reinfection After a Two-stage Revision for Periprosthetic Joint Infection? Results of a Multicenter Case-control Study.
candidates.authors_short: Barbero Allende JM, Fernández E, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reinfection of a joint prosthesis after a two-stage revision is a serious complication, the risk of which may be higher when the procedure is performed after an unsuccessful debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) procedure. The available evidence is scarce and somewhat contradictory, so new studies are required. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Is two-stage revision performed after a prior unsuccessful DAIR associated with a higher risk of prosthetic joint reinfection compared with patients who had no DAIR but rather proceeded directly to two-stage revision? (2) Does the type of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) (acute versus chronic) modify this association? METHODS: We analyzed data from a previous retrospective, case-control study aimed at assessing the risk factors of reinfection of a joint prosthesis treated with two-stage revision in 12 Spanish hospitals between 2009 and 2018. We defined PJI according to the latest criteria published in 2018. We defined "acute PJI" as those occurring early (< 3 months after surgery) and of hematogenous origin and "chronic PJI" as those occurring after 3 months and of nonhematogenous origin. During the period in question, we found 89 cases and selected 171 matched controls. For each case (patients who developed a reinfection of a joint prosthesis within 2 years of reimplantation, based on last internationally accepted consensus criteria), up to two consecutive controls (patients who underwent two-stage revision who did not develop a new infection within 2 years of reimplantation) were included, matched by prosthesis location, center, and year of surgery. There were no differences in age, gender, comorbidities, type of infection, or microbiology between the groups. We analyzed how many patients among cases and controls received a previous DAIR, and we assessed the association of the previous DAIR with reinfection of a joint prosthesis by the OR and its respective 95% confidence interval (CI) obtained through logistic regression, adjusted for potential confounding factors. In addition, we performed a separate analysis depending on whether the PJI was acute or chronic. RESULTS: After adjusting for potentially confounding variables such as age, sex, Charlson comorbidity index, and antibiotic prophylaxis, we found that two-stage revision performed after a prior unsuccessful DAIR was associated with higher odds of prosthetic joint reinfection compared with direct two-stage revision (adjusted OR 3.5 [95% CI 1.4 to 8.8]; p = 0.008). After adjusting for confounders, we found that the odds of reinfection in two-stage revision were higher after unsuccessful DAIR compared with direct two-stage revision in patients with chronic PJI (adjusted OR 4.0 [95% CI 1.4 to 11.3]; p = 0.009) than they were in patients with acute PJI (adjusted OR 2.2 [95% CI 0.7 to 7.2]; p = 0.2), but the interaction test did not show statistical significance. CONCLUSION: Unsuccessful DAIR could be associated with a higher risk of reinfection of a joint prosthesis than in direct two-stage revision. Although no difference was found by the type of infection (acute or chronic), the association might be of greater magnitude in patients with chronic PJI, and future studies should focus on this. Although DAIR is a very attractive therapeutic option for PJI, careful selection of candidate patients is essential to avoid compromising the success of a future two-stage revision. Future prospective studies should confirm these findings and evaluate which poor prognostic factors would weigh against performing a DAIR procedure. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Directly actionable retrospective study of 145 patients identifying optimal plate positioning to reduce hardware irritation after ulnar shortening osteotomy, with specific distance cutoffs to guide surgical technique.
bullets: Patients who failed DAIR before two-stage revision had 3.5 times higher odds of reinfection within two years compared to patients who went directly to two-stage revision.
This increased reinfection risk applies to any patient with periprosthetic joint infection being considered for DAIR, and the risk may be greatest in those with chronic infection.
When selecting patients for DAIR, surgeons should weigh the risk of compromising a future two-stage revision if DAIR fails, particularly in chronic periprosthetic joint infection.

candidates.title: Five-Year Outcomes and Return to Sport After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in Young Patients With Minimal (<10%) or No Glenoid Bone Loss.
candidates.authors_short: Fritsch L, Mitchell BC, et al.
candidates.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Arthroscopic Bankart repair is commonly used to address anterior instability in adolescents and young adults with no or minimal bone loss. However, failure rates remain high, particularly in high-risk populations. PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate clinical outcomes, return-to-sport (RTS) rates, and predictors of failure after arthroscopic Bankart repair in patients ≤24 years of age with minimal glenoid bone loss. It was hypothesized that patients would demonstrate favorable outcomes, low recurrence rates, and high RTS rates, and smaller distance-to-dislocation (DTD) measurements, and contact sports participation would be associated with failure. STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. METHODS: The data of patients with anterior shoulder instability and minimal bone loss (<10%) who underwent primary arthroscopic Bankart repair between 2006 and 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. Remplissage was not performed. Data collected included preoperative instability events, patient-reported outcome measures, satisfaction, radiographic measurements (glenoid bone loss, glenoid track, and DTD), and RTS outcomes. Failure was defined as re-dislocation or recurrent instability requiring surgery. RESULTS: A total of 130 patients were evaluated; 18 were excluded, leaving 112. Of these, 96 patients (85.7%) were available for the final follow-up (mean age, 19.9 ± 3.1 years; mean follow-up, 68.4 ± 42.7 months). All clinical outcomes improved significantly (P < .05) except for the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey Mental Component Summary score. The median satisfaction score was 9 (IQR, 8-10). Participation in contact sports was associated with failure, while other risk factors were not. RTS was achieved by 96.1% of patients; however, only 57.1% returned to their preinjury level. Fewer preoperative dislocation events were associated with successful return to full activity (P = .04). The recurrence rate was 33.3%, and revision surgery was required in 19 patients (19.8%). CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic Bankart repair was associated with high rates of recurrence and revision surgery in a series of patients ≤24 years of age without glenoid bone loss. In those who did not require revision surgery, clinical outcomes and RTS rates were high. Contact sports participation was associated with failure. A greater number of preoperative instability events negatively influence RTS outcomes. Arthroscopic Bankart repair in this population is safe and has a low complication rate, but the failure rate remains considerable.
candidates.score_reasoning: Clinically important 5-year outcomes and return-to-sport data after Bankart repair in 96 young patients from AJSM, though limited by case series design, provides relevant failure rate and predictor data for a high-demand population.
bullets: In patients aged 24 and under with minimal glenoid bone loss, arthroscopic Bankart repair had a 33% recurrence rate and nearly 20% required revision surgery within five years.
Contact sport athletes in this age group had significantly higher failure rates, making them candidates for a more critical surgical selection conversation.
While 96% returned to sport, fewer than 60% returned to their pre-injury level, and more dislocations before surgery predicted worse return-to-sport outcomes.

candidates.title: Multicentric development and validation of a fully automated artificial intelligence system for planning medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy on weight-bearing anterior-posterior long leg radiographs: The ISAKOS John Joyce Award 2025.
candidates.authors_short: Rupp MC, von Schacky CE, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: Preoperative planning, currently performed by orthopaedic surgeons (OS), is essential for successful osteotomy, but is labour-intensive and error-prone. As such, there is significant potential in the use of automated artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to augment the abilities of OS in managing lower extremity pathologies in a high-volume task that demands high precision and reliability. The aim was to develop a deep learning (DL) system capable of fully autonomous planning a medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy (mow-HTO) on weight bearing anterior posterior (AP) long leg radiographs (LLR) and to validate its agreement with an expert-derived reference standard, its reliability and processing time of the DL model compared to expert OS on multicentric test data sets (two institutions). METHODS: A total of 594 patients (age 41.1 ± 13.2 years, 182 female) who underwent osteotomy between 01/2014 and 01/2021 were retrospectively enrolled. Manual annotations for lower extremity alignment and high tibial landmarks were performed on AP LLR radiographs. The data set was divided into training (60%, n = 399), validation (10%, n = 59) and hold-out testing (30%, n = 136), with an additional external dataset (n = 100) for further testing. A DL system with twelve expert networks was trained to identify relevant landmarks for HTO planning. The DL model was then tested on fully automated planning of a medial open wedge HTO based on (1) the desired postoperative intersection of the mechanical axis with the tibial plateau (%-based) and (2) the desired femorotibial axis (°-based). Agreement with the expert-derived reference, reliability and processing time were compared with three expert OS using FDA-approved preoperative planning software on the test data sets. RESULTS: For preoperative alignment parameter analysis, compared to the ground truth, human preoperative accuracy ranged from 0.13° ± 0.10° to 1.06° ± 1.4°, interrater reliability ranged from intraclass correlation (ICC) 0.84-1.0 and clinically acceptable accuracy ranged from 72% to 100%. Preoperative accuracy of the DL model ranged from 0.22° ± 0.18° to 1.04° ± 1.28°, interrater reliability ranged from ICC 0.93-1.0 and clinically acceptable accuracy ranged from 91% to 100%. For the planning of the osteotomy gap, compared to the ground truth, human accuracy ranged from 0.46 ± 0.65 mm to 0.5 ± 0.88 mm (%-based) and 0.43 ± 0.55 to 0.52 ± 0.75 mm (°-based), reliability ranged from ICC 0.9-0.96 and 0.95-0.97 and clinically acceptable accuracy was 93.6%-96.0% (%-based) and 89.8%-93.9% (°-based). For the DL model, the accuracy was 0.53 ± 0.63 mm (%-based) and 0.44 ± 0.53 mm (°-based), reliability was ICC 0.99 (both methods) and clinically acceptable accuracy was 98.1% (%-based) and 96.2% (°-based). The DL-model significantly and substantially outperformed the OS in intrarater reliability (0.88 vs. 1.0) and processing time for a fully automated alignment analysis (25.3 ± 0.8 s vs. 148.7 ± 10.1 s, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The developed DL model enabled fully automated mow-HTO planning on AP long-leg radiographs with reliability comparable to that of expert OS while significantly reducing processing time and improving measurement consistency. These suggest that DL-based systems may assist orthopaedic providers by accelerating and standardising osteotomy planning. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: AJSM RCT with 240 patients and prospective multicenter design showing significantly improved PRP outcomes with a standardized clinical pathway, offering Level 1 evidence for optimizing PRP delivery in early knee OA.
bullets: An AI model planned medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy on long leg radiographs with accuracy matching expert surgeons and clinically acceptable gap calculations in over 96% of cases.
The system completed full alignment analysis in 25 seconds compared to nearly 150 seconds for experienced orthopaedic surgeons, with higher consistency across repeated measurements.
For surgeons performing high volumes of osteotomy planning, this tool could reduce preparation time and standardise preoperative measurements without sacrificing accuracy.

candidates.title: Sepsis Prior to Total Knee Arthroplasty is Associated With Elevated Rates of Myocardial Infarction and Deep Vein Thrombosis.
candidates.authors_short: Alhankawi AR, Holle AM, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients who have sepsis often experience persistent physiological instability, which may increase vulnerability to postoperative complications. However, the impact of preoperative sepsis on outcomes following elective total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains poorly defined. Thus, the purpose of this study was to investigate the association of preoperative sepsis with 90-day and two-year postoperative complications following TKA. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted utilizing an insurance database. Patients who had a preoperative diagnosis of sepsis within two years prior to TKA were matched 1:3 to controls based on demographics and comorbidities. Patients who had sepsis were stratified according to the following timeline: sepsis three months prior to surgery, three to six months prior, six to 12 months prior, 12 to 18 months prior, and 18 to 24 months prior. Medical and surgical complications were assessed at 90 days and two years following surgery. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. RESULTS: Patients who had sepsis within two years prior to surgery exhibited increased rates of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) (odds ratio (OR): 1.6), postoperative sepsis (OR: 2.7), acute kidney injury (OR: 1.4), urinary tract infection (OR: 1.8), blood transfusion (OR: 2.0), readmission (OR: 1.3), and wound dehiscence (OR: 1.4) within 90 days of surgery. At two years following surgery, sepsis was associated with elevated rates of revision surgery (OR: 1.3), PJI (OR: 1.6), osteomyelitis (OR: 1.9), and mortality (OR: 1.3). Sepsis within three months of operation was associated with elevated rates of myocardial infarction (OR: 2.1) and deep vein thrombosis (OR: 2.0). All findings were statistically significant at P < 0.05. CONCLUSION: Preoperative sepsis is associated with increased complications following TKA, including periprosthetic joint infection and mortality. Sepsis within three months of surgery confers a particularly elevated risk of myocardial infarction and deep vein thrombosis following TKA.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large registry-based retrospective cohort from JSES comparing polyethylene versus metallic glenospheres in rTSA across New Zealand Joint Registry data, providing long-term survivorship data relevant to implant selection.
bullets: Patients with sepsis in the two years before TKA face higher rates of periprosthetic joint infection, readmission, revision surgery, and death compared to matched controls.
Sepsis within three months of TKA doubles the risk of myocardial infarction and deep vein thrombosis in the 90-day postoperative period.
Orthopaedic surgeons should carefully weigh timing of elective TKA after sepsis, with particular caution if the episode occurred within the preceding three months.

candidates.title: Postoperative Complications Following Shoulder Stabilization for Primary Versus Recurrent Anterior Shoulder Dislocation: A National Database Study.
candidates.authors_short: Chow AK, Sribhashyam S, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anterior shoulder dislocation (ASD) is the most common joint dislocation in young patients with recurrence rates of nearly 90%. Multiple dislocations can cause progressive structural damage and bone loss, increasing the risk of instability. This study compares recurrence and postoperative complications following ASD between patients with a primary versus recurrent ASD. We hypothesized that surgical stabilization following recurrent ASD would be associated with an increased risk of subsequent instability and a higher complication burden. METHODS: A retrospective query was conducted using the TriNetX database (January 1, 2015 to January 1, 2025) in accordance with STROBE/RECORD guidelines. Patients aged 18 years or older undergoing surgical repair for primary or recurrent ASD were identified. Propensity score matching was applied in a 1:1 ratio and estimated using logistic regression. Postoperative outcomes were evaluated at 3 and 6 months with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction (q=0.05) applied to cohort comparisons. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to assess independent risk factors. RESULTS: Pre-match cohorts included 2,312 patients who underwent surgical repair for primary ASD compared to 7,594 patients in the recurrent ASD cohort; propensity score matching yielded 2,302 patients per group (mean age: 29.7±14.5 years vs. 28.8±13.6 years, respectively). Following Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, recurrent ASD patients experienced significantly higher rates of subsequent dislocation (3-month: 21.4% vs. 1.3%, RD=-20.1%; 6-month: 23.5% vs. 1.7%, RD=-21.8%; both p<0.0001) and shoulder instability (3-month: 44.0% vs. 21.8%, RD=-22.2%; 6-month: 47.8% vs. 24.0%, RD=-23.8%; both p<0.0001). At 6-months, reoperation rates differed between cohorts on unadjusted analysis (2.0% vs. 1.1%, RD=-0.9%, p=0.0159), but the difference did not retain significance following Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q=0.089). No significant differences were observed in shoulder stiffness, rotator cuff tears, shoulder impingement, or shoulder pain. Logistic regression analysis demonstrated that elevated BMI significantly increased odds of postoperative shoulder instability at 3 and 6 months (p=0.022-0.038) in both the primary and recurrent ASD groups. Epilepsy or recurrent seizures were significantly associated with postoperative instability across both time points in primary and recurrent repair groups (p<0.01). CONCLUSION: Patients undergoing surgical repair for recurrent ASD experienced significantly higher short-term rates of recurrent instability compared to those treated for primary ASD. Elevated BMI and seizure disorders were identified as independent risk factors associated with postoperative instability. These findings should be interpreted as associative and hypothesis-generating. Prospective cohort studies incorporating granular imaging and procedure-level data are needed to validate these relationships and evaluate whether surgical selection modifies recurrence risk in high-risk patients. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison using Large Database, Prognosis Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large NSQIP-based development and validation study of the SHORD score in 29,382 TSA patients, providing a practical preoperative bedside tool to predict non-home discharge and optimize patient counseling.
bullets: Patients surgically treated for recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation had roughly 20 times the rate of redislocation within 6 months compared to those treated after a first-time dislocation (23.5% vs. 1.7%).
This applies to adults of all ages undergoing shoulder stabilization surgery, with recurrent dislocators consistently showing higher instability rates at both 3 and 6 months postoperatively.
Elevated BMI and seizure disorders independently increased the risk of postoperative instability in both groups, making these patient factors worth identifying before planning stabilization surgery.

candidates.title: Preoperative Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor Use is Associated With Increased Complication Risk After Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Dose-Response Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Alfonsi SP, Zickler CL, et al.
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Preoperative selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) use has been associated with adverse outcomes following primary total hip arthroplasty (THA). This study examined whether complication rates vary based on SSRI daily dosage. METHODS: A claims database (2010 to 2023) identified 77,958 primary THA patients who did not have osteoporosis and who filled an SSRI prescription 60 days preoperatively. Patients were matched 1:3 to SSRI-naive individuals by age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and history of cognitive disorders, depression, anxiety, and substance use. Overall, 77,958 SSRI users were matched to 233,277 controls (mean age 65 years). After matching, baseline demographics and rates of anxiety and depression (all P > 0.13) were similar between cohorts. The SSRI doses were standardized using quantity, duration, and strength, then stratified as low (0 to 30 mg), medium (30 to 100 mg), or high (greater than 100 mg). Multivariate regression and Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed surgical complications and revision-free survival at 2-year follow-up. RESULTS: Preoperative SSRI use was associated with greater 2-year complications (5.2 versus 3.2%, P < 0.001). In adjusted multivariate analysis, SSRI use was associated with increased odds of component loosening (OR [odds ratio] 1.5), periprosthetic fracture (OR 1.8), periprosthetic joint infection (OR 1.7), dislocation (OR 2.0), and revision surgery (OR 1.7) (all P < 0.001). There was no dose-dependent relationship observed. Component loosening approached statistical significance at high SSRI doses (OR 3.7, P = 0.07). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated reduced revision-free survival among SSRI users (P < 0.001) at 2-year follow-up. CONCLUSION: Preoperative SSRI use, regardless of dose, was associated with higher 2-year rates of periprosthetic joint infection, dislocation, fracture, loosening, and revision. However, the absence of a dose-response relationship suggests that SSRIs are unlikely to be directly responsible for these complications.
candidates.score_reasoning: Retrospective cohort from JSES identifying the medial collapse sign with high sensitivity and specificity for predicting cubitus varus after supracondylar fracture fixation, offering a practical intraoperative radiographic tool despite small sample size.
bullets: THA patients on SSRIs preoperatively had twice the dislocation rate and nearly twice the revision rate at 2 years compared to SSRI-naive patients.
Higher SSRI doses did not produce worse outcomes, suggesting SSRIs are a marker of underlying patient risk rather than a direct cause of complications.
Orthopaedic surgeons should flag preoperative SSRI use as a risk factor for THA complications and counsel patients accordingly, regardless of their dose.

candidates.title: The use of patellar tendon autograft and lateral meniscus repair are associated with loss of motion of the knee among female patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
candidates.authors_short: Dadoo S, Nash AE, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To conduct a sex-stratified analysis of factors associated with subsequent surgery for loss of motion after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), including meniscus repair and graft type. METHODS: All individuals age ≥14 years who underwent primary ACLR between 2014 and 2021 were reviewed. Exclusion criteria included <6 months follow-up and concomitant meniscal root, multiligament, osteochondral or osteotomy procedures. The primary outcome was subsequent surgery for loss of motion. Demographic and surgical variables were compared between individuals who underwent subsequent surgery for loss of motion versus not, for the full cohort and among females and males separately. Significance was set to p < 0.050. RESULTS: A total of 1226 individuals (age: 25 ± 10 years; 49% female) were included at a mean follow-up of 2.3 years. The rate of subsequent surgery for loss of motion was 9.0% for the full cohort, 12.3% for females and 5.9% for males. Among the full cohort, female sex (OR: 2.31; p < 0.001) and lateral meniscus (LM) repair (OR: 1.62; p = 0.048) were predictors of subsequent surgery for loss of motion. Among females, bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) autograft use (OR: 1.91; p = 0.034) and LM repair (OR: 1.72; p = 0.046) were predictors of subsequent surgery for loss of motion, with combined BPTB autograft use and LM repair resulting in a significantly higher rate of subsequent surgery for loss of motion (32% vs. 12%; p = 0.004). Among males, graft type and meniscus repair were not associated with subsequent surgery for loss of motion (both p > 0.050). CONCLUSION: In this sex-stratified analysis, BPTB autograft use and LM repair were identified as factors predictive of subsequent surgery for loss of motion after primary ACLR when analysing females independently, while no predictive factors were identified when analysing males independently. Understanding factors associated with loss of motion after primary ACLR among males and females separately may guide individualised surgical decision-making and patient counselling. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective cohort from KSTA with strong design (Level 2) evaluating serum biomarkers after ACLR versus controls across 12 months, providing biologically relevant mechanistic data about post-ACL cartilage degeneration trajectory.
bullets: Among females undergoing ACL reconstruction, patellar tendon autograft and lateral meniscus repair each independently increase the risk of subsequent surgery for stiffness.
When both patellar tendon autograft and lateral meniscus repair are combined in female patients, the rate of reoperation for stiffness rises to 32%, compared to 12% without that combination.
These risk factors did not apply to male patients, so graft selection and meniscus repair decisions after ACL reconstruction should account for patient sex.

candidates.title: Total Hip Arthroplasty Is Associated With Lower 90-Day Inpatient Readmission Than Hemiarthroplasty for Femoral Neck Fracture in Patients Aged 65-75 Years: A Propensity Score-Matched Nationwide Readmissions Database Study.
candidates.authors_short: Maman D, Steinfeld Y, Berkovich Y
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comparative early hospital-based outcomes of hemiarthroplasty and total hip arthroplasty (THA) for femoral neck fracture remain uncertain in patients aged 65-75 years. METHODS: Using the 2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database, we identified patients aged 65-75 years admitted with an acute femoral neck fracture who underwent hemiarthroplasty or THA. Patients were matched 1:1 using exact matching on age, Hospital Frailty Risk Score category, and mental-disorder status, plus propensity-score matching with a 0.20-standard-deviation caliper. The primary outcome was all-cause inpatient readmission within 90 days. RESULTS: Among 8,012 eligible admissions, 5,108 patients underwent hemiarthroplasty and 2,904 underwent THA. Matching yielded 2,702 patients per group, with all postmatch absolute standardized mean differences <0.10. THA was associated with a lower observed 90-day inpatient readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty (10.1% vs 15.7%; odds ratio, 0.60; 95% confidence interval, 0.51-0.71; P < .001). Death during the first readmission was also less frequent after THA (0.1% vs 0.7%; P = .002). A narrowly defined inpatient principal-diagnosis dislocation indicator did not differ significantly between groups and should not be interpreted as overall dislocation incidence. Index and total 90-day hospital charges were higher with THA. CONCLUSIONS: In this observational claims-based study, THA was associated with a lower observed 90-day inpatient readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty. Residual selection bias may partly explain this association, and these findings do not establish a causal benefit of THA. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective comparative study.

bullets: In patients aged 65 to 75 with femoral neck fracture, THA was associated with a lower 90-day readmission rate than hemiarthroplasty (10.1% vs 15.7%).
Death at first readmission was also less common after THA, though THA carried higher index and total 90-day hospital costs.
For relatively fit patients aged 65 to 75, these findings support considering THA, but selection bias limits causal conclusions and randomised data are still needed.
